subject: sci
title: Science Practices: Questions, Hypotheses, Variables, and Experiment Design
objectives: You will turn an observation into a testable scientific question and write a hypothesis in If…, then…, because… form.
You will identify the independent, dependent, and controlled variables in an experiment description.
You will identify the control group and explain why it is needed.
You will judge whether an experiment is a fair test, checking for repeated trials, sample size, random assignment, placebos, and confounding variables.
You will choose conclusions that are supported by the data in experiment descriptions and data tables.

slides.title: Science Practices: How Scientists Ask and Test Questions
slides.board:
Today you will:

  • Turn an observation into a testable question
  • Write a hypothesis: If…, then…, because…
  • Name the independent, dependent, and controlled variables
  • Find the control group and judge whether a test is fair
  • Draw conclusions that stay inside the data

Plan: Warm-up → 6 big ideas → practice together → your turn → GED-style questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 1 of Science. Many GED Science questions ask how an experiment was set up and what its results show, and you do not need to memorize facts to answer those questions. You need a short list of ideas and a routine, and that is exactly what we build today. By the end of this lesson you will be able to read any experiment description and label its parts in under a minute.
ask: Have you ever tested something at home to see if it worked better, like a cleaning product or a recipe change? (expected answer: any example; use it later as a sample experiment)

slides.title: Readiness Check
slides.board:
1. Which statement can be settled by measuring?
    (a) Blue cars are the prettiest cars.
    (b) Blue cars get hotter inside in the sun than white cars.
  2. Find the mean of 12, 15, and 18 minutes.
  3. A plant was 4.0 cm tall on Monday and 7.5 cm tall on Friday. How much did it grow?
  4. On a graph, which axis runs left to right?
steps: 1. (b). You can measure the temperature inside each car. Statement (a) is an opinion; no measurement settles it.
2. (12 + 15 + 18) ÷ 3 = 45 ÷ 3 = 15 minutes.
3. 7.5 − 4.0 = 3.5 cm.
4. The x-axis runs left to right (horizontal). The y-axis runs up and down.

notes.say: These four problems check the skills this lesson leans on: telling a measurable claim from an opinion, finding a mean, reading a change, and knowing the axes of a graph. Give the student about two minutes, then have them tell you each answer before you reveal it. If the mean or the axes are shaky, take a minute now, because both come back later today.
ask: Why can't we test statement (a)? (expected answer: it is an opinion; there is nothing to measure)
How do you find a mean? (expected answer: add the values, divide by how many values there are)
notes.answer: 1. (b) is testable; (a) is an opinion. 2. 15 minutes. 3. 3.5 cm. 4. The x-axis.
notes.watch: For the mean, some students divide by 2 or forget to divide. Have them say the count out loud: three values, so divide by 3.

slides.title: Big Idea 1: Observations and Testable Questions
slides.board:
Observation: something you notice with your senses or a measuring tool.

Testable question: names something you can change and something you can measure.

TestableNot testable
Does water temperature affect how fast sugar dissolves?Is summer the nicest season?
Do bean plants grow taller with more fertilizer?Should people eat more beans?

notes.say: Science starts when someone notices something and asks why. But not every question can be answered by science. A testable question has two parts you can point to: one thing you can change, and one thing you can measure. Questions about what is best, nicest, or what people should do are opinions or values, so no experiment can settle them.
ask: In the sugar question, what would you change and what would you measure? (expected answer: change water temperature; measure time to dissolve)
Why is 'Should people eat more beans?' not testable? (expected answer: it asks what people should do, which is a value judgment, not a measurement)
notes.watch: Students sometimes think any question with a science word is testable. Ask: "What would you measure?" If there is no answer, it is not testable.

slides.title: Worked Example: From Observation to Question
slides.board:
Observation: After a rainstorm, puddles in the sun dry up faster than puddles in the shade.

Write a testable question about this observation.
steps: Find a possible cause: the sunny puddles get direct sunlight, which warms the water; the shaded puddles do not.
Name the change and the measurement. Change: sunlight or shade. Measure: time for the water to evaporate.
Write the question: Does the amount of sunlight affect how long it takes a puddle of water to evaporate?
Check it: it names one change and one measurement, and it is not an opinion. It is testable.

notes.say: Watch how I go from something I noticed to a question I can test. First I look for a difference between the two situations that might explain what I saw. Then I name what I would change and what I would measure, and I build the question from those two pieces. That last check, 'can I point to the change and the measurement?', is the test for every question.
ask: What else might differ between the two puddles? (expected answer: the size of the puddle, the surface under it, wind; good, those could be other questions or things to control)

slides.title: Big Idea 2: The Hypothesis
slides.board:
If [what I change], then [what I expect to measure], because [my reason].

  • A hypothesis is a testable prediction, not a question and not a wild guess.
  • After the experiment, the data support or do not support it.
  • One experiment never "proves" a hypothesis.

notes.say: A hypothesis is your best prediction, stated so it can be tested. The If part names the change, the then part names the result you will measure, and the because part gives your reason. Notice the language at the bottom: scientists say the data support or do not support a hypothesis. One experiment can be wrong for many reasons, so we never say it proves anything, and the GED likes to test that word.
ask: Is 'Does fertilizer help plants grow?' a hypothesis? (expected answer: no, it is a question; it makes no prediction)
notes.watch: The most common error is writing the question again with a period at the end. Insist on the If…then form until it becomes automatic.

slides.title: Worked Example: Write the Hypothesis
slides.board:
Question: Does the amount of sunlight affect how long it takes a puddle of water to evaporate?

Write a hypothesis in If…, then…, because… form.
steps: If = the change: If a puddle gets direct sunlight,
then = the measured result: then it will evaporate in less time than a puddle in the shade,
because = the reason: because sunlight warms the water, and warmer water evaporates faster.
Test it: pour the same amount of water into identical pans, set one in the sun and one in the shade, and time how long each takes to dry. The prediction can be checked, so it is a good hypothesis.

notes.say: I build the hypothesis straight from the question. The change goes after If, the measurement goes after then, and I add a reason I can explain. Then I ask myself how I would test it; if I can describe the test, the hypothesis is testable.
ask: Could the data turn out to not support this hypothesis? What would that look like? (expected answer: yes, if the sunny pan took as long or longer to dry)

slides.title: We Do: Question to Hypothesis
slides.board:
Write a hypothesis for each question.

  1. Does the number of hours of sunlight per day affect how tall sunflowers grow?
  2. Does adding salt to water change the temperature at which the water freezes?
steps: 1. If sunflowers get more hours of sunlight each day, then they will grow taller, because plants use light energy to make their food.
2. If salt is added to water, then the water will freeze at a lower temperature, because dissolved salt gets in the way of water particles locking together into ice.
Check both: each one names the change (sunlight; salt), the measurement (height; freezing temperature), and a reason.

notes.say: Let's do these together. You tell me the If part first, then the then part, and I will write them as you talk. The reason does not have to be perfect science yet, but it should connect the change to the result. For the second one, you may already know the answer from real life: that is why salt goes on icy roads.
ask: What is the If part for number 1? (expected answer: if sunflowers get more hours of sunlight)
What will we measure in number 2? (expected answer: the temperature at which the water freezes)
notes.answer: Any hypothesis that predicts how the change affects the measured result is acceptable. Model answers: 1. If sunflowers get more hours of sunlight each day, then they will grow taller, because plants use light to make food. 2. If salt is added to water, then the water will freeze at a lower temperature, because dissolved salt interferes with ice forming. (Dissolved salt does lower the freezing point.)
notes.watch: Watch for a hypothesis with no direction, such as "sunlight will affect height." Push for which way: taller or shorter?

slides.title: Big Idea 3: Variables
slides.board:
VariableWhat it isAsk
Independent (IV)The one thing changed on purposeWhat did they choose to change?
Dependent (DV)What is measured; the resultWhat did they measure?
ControlledKept the same for every groupWhat stayed the same?

DRY MIX: Dependent, Responding, Y-axis. Manipulated, Independent, X-axis.

notes.say: A variable is anything that can change in an experiment. The independent variable is the cause being tested, the one thing the scientist sets on purpose. The dependent variable is the effect, what the scientist waits for and measures, so it depends on the independent variable. Everything else is held the same so it cannot muddy the result; those are the controlled variables. DRY MIX tells you which goes on which axis of a graph, and a quick sentence check is: the effect of the independent variable on the dependent variable.
ask: In the sugar experiment, which is the IV and which is the DV? (expected answer: IV water temperature; DV time to dissolve)
Which axis gets the dependent variable? (expected answer: the y-axis)
notes.watch: Students often pick the most interesting variable as the independent one. Ask: "Which one did the scientist decide before the experiment started?" That is the IV.

slides.title: Worked Example: Label the Paper Towel Test
slides.board: A student cuts one 10 cm × 10 cm square from each of three paper towel brands (A, B, C). She dips each square in room-temperature water for 10 seconds, lets it drip for 30 seconds, squeezes it into a measuring cup, and records the volume. She does this three times for each brand.
steps: IV (changed on purpose): the brand of paper towel.
DV (measured): the volume of water absorbed, in mL.
Controlled: square size, dip time, drip time, water temperature, squeezing method.
Control group: none. She compares brands with each other; not every experiment has a no-treatment group.
Three trials per brand so one odd square cannot decide the result; she should average them.

notes.say: Here is the routine I want you to use every time. First, what did she change on purpose? The brand. Second, what did she measure? The volume of water. Third, what did she keep the same? Everything else in the procedure. Notice there is no control group here, and that is fine, because she is comparing brands to each other.
ask: Say it as a sentence: the effect of ___ on ___. (expected answer: the effect of brand on volume of water absorbed)

slides.title: We Do: Coffee and Reaction Time
slides.board:
Volunteers drink 0, 1, 2, or 3 cups of coffee. Thirty minutes later, each person's reaction time is measured with the same computer test in the same quiet room.

  1. Name the IV.
  2. Name the DV.
  3. Name two controlled variables.
  4. Which variable goes on the x-axis of a graph?
steps: 1. IV: the number of cups of coffee.
2. DV: reaction time.
3. Any two: the 30-minute wait, the same computer test, the same quiet room (also the cup size and type of coffee, if kept the same).
4. The IV, number of cups, goes on the x-axis (Manipulated, Independent, X).

notes.say: Your turn to lead, with me as backup. Read the description and tell me what was chosen ahead of time and what was measured afterward. Then find the conditions that stayed the same for everyone. Finally, use DRY MIX for the graph question.
ask: Which group would be the baseline here? (expected answer: the people who drank 0 cups)
notes.answer: 1. Number of cups of coffee. 2. Reaction time. 3. Any two of: wait time (30 minutes), same computer test, same room, same cup size or coffee type. 4. Number of cups of coffee goes on the x-axis; reaction time goes on the y-axis.
notes.watch: If the student says "coffee" for the IV, push for the variable: the number of cups of coffee. Variables are amounts or categories that can change.

slides.title: Big Idea 4: The Control Group
slides.board:
• Control group: does not get the treatment (or gets the normal condition). It is the baseline.
  • Experimental groups: get the treatment being tested.
  • Controlled variables: conditions kept the same for all groups.

Control group = plants, people, or objects. Controlled variables = conditions like time, temperature, amount of water.

notes.say: The control group answers the question: what happens without the treatment? Without it, you cannot tell whether the treatment did anything, because the plants might have grown that much anyway. The words control group and controlled variables sound alike, and the GED counts on you mixing them up. A group is made of things; a controlled variable is a condition you hold steady.
ask: In a fertilizer test with 0, 5, 10, and 15 mL, which is the control group? (expected answer: the 0 mL group)
Is 'all plants get 100 mL of water' a control group or a controlled variable? (expected answer: a controlled variable)
notes.watch: Some students choose the group with the best result as the control. The control is chosen before the experiment; results do not decide it.

slides.title: Worked Example: Jumping Jacks and Heart Rate
slides.board: Twenty adults are randomly split into two groups of 10. Group 1 does jumping jacks for 5 minutes. Group 2 sits quietly for 5 minutes. Each person's heart rate (beats per minute) is measured right afterward.
steps: Hypothesis: If a person does 5 minutes of jumping jacks, then the person's heart rate will be higher than if the person sat quietly, because working muscles need more oxygen.
IV: activity (jumping jacks or sitting). DV: heart rate in beats per minute.
Control group: Group 2, who sit quietly. They show heart rate without the exercise.
Controlled variables: 5 minutes, the same way and time of measuring, the same room.
Random assignment makes the groups alike in fitness and age, so activity is the only real difference.

notes.say: Here the treatment is exercise, so the control group is the group that does not exercise. Notice the difference between Group 2, which is people, and the 5-minute time limit, which is a condition kept the same for both groups. The random split matters too: if the coach had put all the athletes in one group, fitness would be a second difference.
ask: Why not just measure Group 1 and skip Group 2? (expected answer: without a baseline, we would not know whether their heart rate was actually higher than normal)

slides.title: Your Turn: Variables and Control Groups
slides.board:
1. A scientist tests a new soap. Some plates of bacteria get the new soap, some get regular soap, and some get only water. Which plates are the control group?
  2. A runner times her mile in three different types of shoes. Name the IV and the DV.
  3. Forty tomato plants are randomly split. Group A gets a new plant food; Group B gets plain water. After 6 weeks, the tomatoes on each plant are counted. Name the control group and one controlled variable.
steps: 1. The plates that get only water: no soap at all, the baseline.
2. IV: type of shoe. DV: time to run one mile.
3. Control group: Group B (plain water). Controlled variable: any condition kept the same, such as the 6 weeks, the amount of water, sunlight, or soil.

notes.say: Work these alone; you have three minutes. Tell me your answers when you are done, and tell me how you decided. I will only reveal the answers after you commit.
notes.answer: 1. The water-only plates (the regular-soap plates are a useful comparison, but the water-only plates are the no-treatment baseline). 2. IV: type of shoe; DV: mile time. 3. Control group: Group B, the plain-water plants; controlled variable: growing time, water amount, light, soil, or pot size.
notes.watch: On problem 1, students may say the regular-soap plates. Ask: "Which plates get no soap treatment at all?"

slides.title: Big Idea 5: Is It a Fair Test?
slides.board:
• Change only one variable at a time.
  • Repeat trials or use many subjects; average the results.
  • Randomly assign subjects to groups so the groups start out alike.
  • Look for a confounding variable: a second difference between groups that could explain the result.
  • With people: use a placebo and do not tell subjects their group.

notes.say: A fair test is set up so that the only explanation left for the result is the independent variable. If two things change at once, you cannot tell which one caused the result; that second difference is called a confounding variable. One plant or one person can be unusual, so we repeat trials and use groups, then take the mean. With people, expectations alone can change results, so we give the control group a placebo, a fake treatment that looks real.
ask: What question should you ask about any two groups being compared? (expected answer: besides the independent variable, how else were they different?)
notes.watch: Students accept a conclusion because it sounds reasonable. Train the habit: always hunt for a second difference before agreeing.

slides.title: Worked Example: Spot the Flaw and Fix It
slides.board: A homeowner spreads a new fertilizer on his front lawn, which gets full sun all day. He puts nothing on his back lawn, which is shaded by trees. After 4 weeks, the front lawn is greener and thicker. He concludes the fertilizer works.
steps: IV: fertilizer or no fertilizer. DV: how green and thick the grass is.
Flaw: the lawns also differ in sunlight. Sunlight is a confounding variable; it could explain the result by itself.
Fix: use one lawn with even sunlight. Mark off several equal plots and randomly choose half to fertilize; the rest are the control.
Water every plot the same, measure each the same way (for example, count blades in a small square), and compare the averages.

notes.say: This is the kind of flaw the GED loves. The homeowner's conclusion sounds fine until you ask how else the two lawns differ, and then the sunlight jumps out. The fix always does the same thing: make the groups alike in every way except the independent variable.
ask: Name one more possible confounding variable here. (expected answer: soil type, foot traffic, or how much each lawn is watered)

slides.title: Worked Example: Repeated Trials and the Mean
slides.board:
A student times how long an ice cube takes to melt in a cup of 30 °C water. Her three trials: 95 s, 101 s, 98 s.

  1. Find the mean.
  2. Why run three trials instead of one?
steps: Add the trials: 95 + 101 + 98 = 294.
Divide by the number of trials: 294 ÷ 3 = 98 seconds.
Why three trials: any single trial can be off (a slightly larger ice cube, a draft in the room). The mean of several trials is more reliable than one result.
Same idea with living things: a group of several plants is more reliable than one plant, which might have a weak seed.

notes.say: GED Science gives you an on-screen calculator, and mean-of-trials questions are common fill-in items. The method is always the same: add, then divide by how many trials there were. The bigger idea is why we repeat at all: repeating protects us from one unusual result.
ask: If she had divided by 4 by mistake, what would she get? (expected answer: 73.5, which is lower than every trial, a sign something is wrong)
notes.watch: Teach the sanity check: a mean must land between the smallest and largest values. 294 or 73.5 cannot be right.

slides.title: We Do: The Calm-Music Study
slides.board:
A nurse randomly assigns 60 patients waiting for minor surgery into two groups of 30. One group listens to calm music through headphones for 20 minutes. The other group wears the same headphones for 20 minutes with no sound. Blood pressure is measured before and after.

  1. IV and DV?
  2. Which group is the control group?
  3. Why do the controls wear silent headphones instead of none?
  4. Why random assignment?
steps: 1. IV: whether the patient hears calm music. DV: change in blood pressure.
2. Control: the 30 patients with silent headphones.
3. So the only difference is the music. Resting quietly with headphones on might relax people by itself; now that effect is the same in both groups. (It works like a placebo.)
4. So the groups start out alike in age, health, and nervousness; this prevents a confounding variable.

notes.say: This study is well designed, and I want you to see why. Walk me through it with the same routine: changed, measured, kept the same, control group. Question 3 is the deep one; think about what wearing headphones and sitting still for 20 minutes might do even without music.
ask: Name two controlled variables. (expected answer: 20 minutes, the same headphones, the timing of measurements, the same blood-pressure equipment)
notes.answer: 1. IV: calm music or no music; DV: change in blood pressure. 2. The silent-headphones group. 3. It makes music the only difference between groups, so any relaxation from sitting quietly with headphones is the same for both. 4. Random assignment makes the groups similar at the start, so no second difference explains the result.

slides.title: Big Idea 6: Drawing Conclusions from Data
slides.board:
• Describe the pattern: as the IV goes up, what does the DV do?
  • Say whether the data support or do not support the hypothesis.
  • Stay inside the data. A test from 10 °C to 55 °C says little about 100 °C.
  • Every part of a conclusion must be shown in the table or graph. Words like always, only, and proves are red flags.

notes.say: The last step of an experiment is the conclusion, and this is where many GED answer choices go wrong. The right conclusion describes the pattern the data actually show and nothing more. A wrong choice often adds something extra: a claim about conditions that were never tested, or a word like always or only that the data cannot back up.
ask: If plants were tested with 0 to 20 mL of fertilizer, can we say what 50 mL would do? (expected answer: no, that is outside the tested range)

slides.title: Worked Example: Read the Compost Data
slides.board:
Hypothesis: If tomato plants get more compost, then they will produce more tomatoes.

Compost per pot (cups)01234
Mean tomatoes per plant1014171915
steps: Read in order of the IV: 10 → 14 → 17 → 19 (rising), then 15 (falling).
Pattern: the tomato count rose from 0 to 3 cups, then dropped at 4 cups.
Conclusion: the data support the hypothesis from 0 to 3 cups but not at 4 cups, where more compost was linked to fewer tomatoes.
Compare with the control: the 3-cup plants made 19 − 10 = 9 more tomatoes on average than the 0-cup plants.

notes.say: Always read data in the order of the independent variable, left to right. Here the pattern rises and then falls, so a conclusion that says 'more compost always means more tomatoes' is wrong. A careful conclusion says exactly where the pattern holds and where it breaks.
ask: Did the 4-cup plants make fewer tomatoes than the control? (expected answer: no; 15 is still more than 10)

slides.title: Your Turn: Fair Test or Not?
slides.board:
For each, name the problem.

  1. A student tests whether ball size affects how far a ball rolls. She rolls a small ball on carpet and a large ball on tile.
  2. A study gives a new medicine to young volunteers and a sugar pill to older volunteers.
  3. A student grows one sunflower under each of four light settings.
steps: 1. Two variables changed at once: ball size and floor surface. The surface is a confounding variable. Roll both balls on the same surface.
2. Age is a confounding variable: the groups differ in age as well as treatment. Volunteers should be randomly assigned.
3. Only one plant per condition; one weak plant could mislead. Use several plants per condition and average.

notes.say: Three minutes, on your own. For each one, use the question: besides the independent variable, how else are the groups different, or what makes the result unreliable?
notes.answer: 1. Surface is a second variable (confounding); use one surface. 2. Age differs between groups (confounding); randomly assign volunteers. 3. Sample size of one; use several plants per light setting and find the mean.

slides.title: Your Turn: Conclusions from a Table
slides.board:
Hypothesis: If water is warmer, then an antacid tablet will dissolve faster.

Water temperature (°C)10203040
Mean time to dissolve (s)75523829
  1. Describe the pattern.
  2. Do the data support the hypothesis?
  3. How many seconds faster did the tablet dissolve at 40 °C than at 10 °C?
  4. Can you conclude how long it takes at 90 °C?
steps: 1. As water temperature increases, the dissolving time decreases.
2. Yes, the data support it: less time means faster dissolving, at every temperature tested.
3. 75 − 29 = 46 seconds faster.
4. No. 90 °C is far outside the tested range (10–40 °C). You could only guess it would likely be faster still.

notes.say: Four quick ones. Watch the trap in question 2: the numbers go down, but down here means faster, so the data support the hypothesis. Tell me your answers, then we reveal.
notes.answer: 1. Time decreases as temperature increases. 2. Yes, supported at every temperature tested. 3. 46 seconds. 4. No, 90 °C was not tested; the conclusion must stay within 10–40 °C.
notes.watch: Students see falling numbers and say "not supported." Ask: "Does less time mean faster or slower?"

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Find the Weakness
slides.board:
A teacher tests whether a new reading app improves reading scores. Her morning class uses the app for 8 weeks; her afternoon class does not. The morning class's average score rises 12 points; the afternoon class's rises 4 points.

Which is the biggest weakness of this study?

A. The classes may differ in other ways, because students were not randomly assigned.
B. Reading score was used as the dependent variable the teacher measured.
C. The afternoon class served as a control group that did not use the app.
D. The results were reported as class averages instead of individual scores.
steps: B is out. Naming reading score as the dependent variable is correct, not a weakness; every study measures something.
C is out. Having a control group is a strength. Without the afternoon class, we would have no baseline.
D is out. Averages are the right way to compare groups; they reduce the effect of one unusual student.
A is correct. Morning and afternoon classes differ in time of day and in who signed up for them. Those are confounding variables, so the app may not explain the extra 8 points.

notes.say: Here is how GED questions about design usually look. Read the stem, then go through each choice and ask whether it is actually a problem. Two of these wrong choices describe things that are correct parts of a good study, which is a common trick.
ask: What would fix the weakness? (expected answer: randomly assign students from both classes to use or not use the app)
notes.answer: A. The groups were not randomly assigned, so time of day and class makeup are confounding variables. B, C, and D describe normal, correct features of a study.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Best-Supported Conclusion
slides.board:
Hours of light per day481216
Mean pea plant height (cm)8141921

Which conclusion is best supported?

A. Pea plants grew taller with more light, but the gain was smaller above 12 hours.
B. Pea plants given 24 hours of light will grow the tallest.
C. Light is the only factor that affects pea plant height.
D. Plants with 16 hours of light grew twice as tall as plants with 8 hours.
steps: B is out. 24 hours was never tested; it goes beyond the data.
C is out. The experiment tested only light. It cannot show that nothing else matters; "only" is a red flag.
D is out. 14 cm × 2 = 28 cm, but the 16-hour plants were 21 cm. That is 1.5 times as tall, not twice.
A is correct. Gains were 6 cm (4→8 h), 5 cm (8→12 h), then only 2 cm (12→16 h).

notes.say: Conclusion questions reward the most careful answer, not the most exciting one. Eliminate anything that goes beyond the tested range, anything with an absolute word, and anything that misreads the numbers. Whatever is left should match the table exactly.
ask: Which choice did the math check eliminate? (expected answer: D; 21 is not twice 14)
notes.answer: A. Height rose 8 → 14 → 19 → 21 cm, with the smallest gain (2 cm) from 12 to 16 hours. B extrapolates, C overclaims, D miscalculates (21 ÷ 14 = 1.5).

slides.title: Test Strategy: Label Before You Answer
slides.board:
Before reading the choices, jot three labels on your scratch paper:

C = what was changed (IV)
M = what was measured (DV)
S = what stayed the same (controlled variables + control group)

About 20 seconds. Wrong choices usually swap these roles.

Then ask: How else were the groups different?

notes.say: This is the habit I want you to take into the test. When you see an experiment, spend twenty seconds labeling C, M, and S before you even look at the answers. Most wrong choices on design questions simply swap the roles, calling the measured thing the independent variable, or a controlled variable the control group, and your labels catch that instantly. Then ask the confounding question before you trust any conclusion.
ask: Label the paper towel test: C, M, S. (expected answer: C brand; M water absorbed; S square size, dip time, drip time, water temperature)

slides.title: Recap and What Comes Next
slides.board:
1. A testable question names a change and a measurement.
  2. Hypothesis: If…, then…, because…. Data support it or do not; they never prove it.
  3. IV = changed (x-axis). DV = measured (y-axis). Controlled = kept the same.
  4. Control group = the baseline with no treatment. A fair test changes one thing, repeats trials, randomly assigns, and has no confounding variables.
  5. Conclusions stay inside the data.

Next: Student Lesson → Practice (Set A) → Exit Check

notes.say: Let's pull it together. Read each takeaway back to me in your own words. Your next step is the Student Lesson, which walks through every idea again with a check on each screen. Then do Practice Set A; if you score under 80 percent, take Set B. Finish with the Exit Check, where you need 6 of 8.
ask: What is the difference between a control group and a controlled variable? (expected answer: a control group is a group with no treatment; controlled variables are conditions kept the same for all groups)
Why do scientists repeat trials? (expected answer: so one unusual result does not mislead them)

screens.title: What you will learn
screens.html:
On the GED Science test, many questions describe an experiment and ask how it was set up or what its results show. You do not need to memorize lots of facts to answer them. You need a few clear ideas and a routine. In this lesson you will learn to:

  • Turn an observation into a testable question.
  • Write a hypothesis in If…, then…, because… form.
  • Name the independent, dependent, and controlled variables.
  • Find the control group and explain why it is needed.
  • Judge whether an experiment is a fair test.
  • Choose a conclusion that the data actually support.

Each screen teaches one idea and ends with a quick check. Take your time; you can use the hint if you get stuck.

screens.title: Observations and testable questions
screens.html:
Science begins with an observation: something you notice with your senses or a measuring tool. Then you ask a question about it.

A scientific question must be testable. That means you can point to two things in it:

  • something you can change, and
  • something you can measure.

"Does the temperature of water affect how fast sugar dissolves?" is testable: change the water temperature, measure the time. "Is summer the nicest season?" is not testable. It is an opinion, and no measurement can settle it. Questions about what is best, prettiest, or what people should do are not scientific questions.

check.prompt: Which question could be answered by doing an experiment?
options: Does the amount of salt in water affect how long it takes to boil?
Which kitchen spice tastes the best?
Should every family own a vegetable garden?
Why are some people so afraid of spiders even though most spiders are harmless?
why: "Tastes the best" is an opinion. Nothing can be changed and measured to settle it. Look for a question with a change (salt amount) and a measurement (boiling time).
"Should" asks what people ought to do, which is a value judgment, not something you can measure. A testable question names a change and a measurement.
This question does not name anything you would change on purpose or a measurement that would answer it. A testable question names both.
check.hint: Look for the question where you could change one thing and measure the result.
check.explain: Only the salt question names something to change (the amount of salt) and something to measure (the time to boil). The spice and garden questions ask for opinions or values. The spider question is interesting, but as written it names nothing to change and nothing to measure.

screens.title: From observation to question
screens.html:
To turn an observation into a testable question, use three moves:

  1. Find a difference between the situations that might explain what you saw.
  2. Name what you would change and what you would measure.
  3. Put them together: Does [the change] affect [the measurement]?

Then check your question: can you point to the change and the measurement? If either one is missing, rewrite it until both are there.

example.prompt: Observation: After a rainstorm, puddles in the sun dry up faster than puddles in the shade. Write a testable question.
steps: Difference: the sunny puddles get direct sunlight; the shaded ones do not.
Change: sunlight or shade. Measure: time for the water to evaporate.
Question: Does the amount of sunlight affect how long it takes a puddle of water to evaporate?
example.answer: Does the amount of sunlight affect how long it takes a puddle of water to evaporate?

check.prompt: Kia notices that the ice in her insulated cup lasts longer than the ice in her plain plastic cup. Which is the best testable question based on her observation?
options: Does the type of cup affect how long it takes ice to melt?
Is an insulated cup a better choice than a plain plastic cup for cold drinks?
How much ice did Kia put into each of her two cups this morning?
Does ice melt?
why: "Better" is not a measurement. Better at what? A testable question must name what you will measure, such as melting time.
This asks for one measurement but does not connect it to anything being changed. Her observation is about cup type and melting time.
Everyone already knows ice melts. This question has no change to test and does not match her observation about the two cups.
check.hint: Her observation compares two cups. What would she change, and what would she time?
check.explain: The change is the type of cup and the measurement is how long the ice takes to melt. "Does the type of cup affect how long it takes ice to melt?" names both. "Is an insulated cup a better choice?" sounds close, but "better" is not something you can measure until you say better at what.

screens.title: The hypothesis
screens.html:
A hypothesis is a testable prediction that answers your question. It is not a question, and it is not a wild guess. Use this frame:

If [what you change], then [what you expect to measure], because [your reason].

The If part names the change. The then part names the result you will measure and which way you expect it to go. The because part explains your thinking.

example.prompt: Question: Does the amount of sunlight affect how long it takes a puddle of water to evaporate? Write a hypothesis.
steps: If: If a puddle gets direct sunlight,
then: then it will evaporate in less time than a puddle in the shade,
because: because sunlight warms the water, and warmer water evaporates faster.
example.answer: If a puddle gets direct sunlight, then it will evaporate in less time than a puddle in the shade, because sunlight warms the water and warmer water evaporates faster.

check.prompt: Read Andre's notes. Click the sentence that states his hypothesis.
spans: Andre noticed that his phone battery seemed to drain faster on cold mornings.
He wondered whether temperature affects how long a phone battery lasts.
If a phone is kept at a colder temperature, then its battery will run down in fewer hours.
He plans to play the same video on two identical phones, one at 5 °C and one at 22 °C.
He will record how many hours each battery lasts.
check.why: Many people click "He wondered whether temperature affects…" That sentence is the question. A hypothesis makes a prediction, usually in If…then form.
check.hint: A hypothesis predicts what will happen. Look for an If…then statement.
check.explain: The hypothesis is the prediction: "If a phone is kept at a colder temperature, then its battery will run down in fewer hours." The first sentence is an observation, the second is the question, and the last two describe the procedure.

screens.title: Support, not prove
screens.html:
After an experiment, you compare the results with your hypothesis.

  • If the results match the prediction, the data support the hypothesis.
  • If they do not match, the data do not support it.

Scientists do not say one experiment proves a hypothesis. A single experiment might have a hidden flaw, a small sample, or a lucky result. Other scientists need to repeat it. A hypothesis that is not supported is not a failure either; it still teaches you something.

On the GED, an answer choice that says an experiment "proves" something is usually a trap.

check.prompt:
Andre's hypothesis was: If a phone is kept colder, then its battery will run down in fewer hours. The phone at 5 °C lasted 6.5 hours, and the phone at 22 °C lasted 9 hours.

These results {{0}} Andre's hypothesis. A scientist would say this test {{1}}.

options: support
do not support
disprove
why: The cold phone lasted fewer hours (6.5 vs. 9), which is exactly what Andre predicted. The results match, so they support it.
The results agree with the prediction, so nothing was disproved. Also, one test is not enough to disprove or prove a hypothesis.

options: proves that cold always drains batteries
provides evidence for the hypothesis, but should be repeated
shows temperature is the only thing that affects battery life
why: One test with two phones cannot prove anything, and "always" goes far beyond the data. Scientists say the data support a hypothesis.
The test changed only temperature. It cannot show that nothing else (screen brightness, battery age) matters.

check.hint: Did the cold phone last fewer hours? And can one test ever prove something?
check.explain: The cold phone lasted 6.5 hours, fewer than the 9 hours at 22 °C, so the results support the hypothesis. With only one phone per temperature, the test provides evidence but should be repeated. It does not prove anything, and it cannot show temperature is the only factor.

screens.title: Independent and dependent variables
screens.html:
A variable is anything that can change in an experiment.

  • The independent variable (IV) is the one thing the scientist changes on purpose. It is the cause being tested. Ask: What did they choose to change?
  • The dependent variable (DV) is what the scientist measures to see the effect. It depends on the IV. Ask: What did they measure?

A handy check sentence: "the effect of [IV] on [DV]."

example.prompt: A student sets identical ice cubes on plates made of metal, plastic, and wood, all at room temperature, and times how long each cube takes to melt. Name the IV and DV.
steps: What did she choose to change? The plate material. That is the IV.
What did she measure? The time to melt. That is the DV.
Check: "the effect of plate material on melting time." It makes sense.
example.answer: IV: plate material. DV: time for the ice cube to melt.

check.prompt: A gardener wants to know whether the type of mulch affects how moist soil stays. She covers three identical garden beds with straw, wood chips, or shredded leaves, waters each bed with 10 liters, and measures the soil moisture 3 days later. What is the dependent variable?
options: The soil moisture after 3 days
The type of mulch
The amount of water each bed gets
The size of each garden bed
why: The type of mulch is what she changes on purpose, so it is the independent variable, not the dependent one.
Every bed gets the same 10 liters, so water is a controlled variable, not what she measures.
The beds are identical, so bed size is a controlled variable. She measures moisture, not size.
check.hint: The dependent variable is what she measures at the end.
check.explain: She measures the soil moisture after 3 days, so moisture is the dependent variable. Mulch type is what she changes (independent). The water amount and bed size stay the same (controlled).

screens.title: DRY MIX: variables on a graph
screens.html:
When results are graphed, each variable has a home:

Dependent = Responding = Y-axis (up and down)
Manipulated = Independent = X-axis (left to right)

"Manipulated" means changed on purpose. "Responding" means it responds to the change. So if a graph shows fertilizer amount along the bottom and plant height up the side, fertilizer is the IV and height is the DV.

You can use this in reverse on the GED: if you are shown a graph, the variable on the x-axis is usually the one the scientist changed.

check.prompt: A scientist tests how the number of hours of light per day affects the height of pea plants. On a graph of the results, hours of light goes on the {{0}}, and plant height goes on the {{1}}.

options: x-axis
y-axis
graph key
why: Hours of light is what the scientist changes (manipulated, independent), and the independent variable goes on the x-axis: M-I-X.
A key only names the data series. The variable the scientist changes is placed along the x-axis: M-I-X.

options: x-axis
y-axis
graph key
why: Plant height is what is measured (dependent, responding), so it goes on the y-axis: D-R-Y.
A key only names the data series. The measured variable is plotted up the y-axis: D-R-Y.

check.hint: Which one did the scientist change? Use DRY MIX.
check.explain: Hours of light is changed on purpose, so it is the independent variable and goes on the x-axis. Plant height is measured, so it is the dependent variable and goes on the y-axis.

screens.title: Controlled variables
screens.html:
Controlled variables (also called constants) are all the conditions kept the same for every group. If they changed, they could affect the result and you would not know what caused it.

In the ice cube experiment, the size of the cubes, the room temperature, and the size of the plates are all controlled. Only the plate material changes.

To find controlled variables, read the procedure and look for words like same, identical, each, every, or a fixed amount given for all groups ("200 mL of water," "12 hours of light").

check.prompt:
A student tests whether the color of light affects how fast algae grow. Each tank gets a different color of light. All tanks hold 2 liters of the same pond water and are kept at 24 °C. After 10 days she measures the amount of algae in each tank.

Which two are controlled variables? Select two.
options: The volume of pond water in each tank
The color of light each tank gets
The amount of algae after 10 days
The water temperature
The kinds of fish in the pond
why: Light color is different for each tank on purpose, so it is the independent variable, not a controlled one.
The amount of algae is what she measures at the end, so it is the dependent variable.
Fish are never mentioned. They are not something she kept the same or measured, so they are not part of this design.
check.hint: Controlled variables are the conditions that are the same for every tank.
check.explain: Every tank held the same volume of water (2 liters) at the same temperature (24 °C), so those are controlled variables. Light color changes on purpose (IV) and the amount of algae is measured (DV).

screens.title: The control group
screens.html:
Many experiments compare groups. The control group does not get the treatment being tested, or it gets the normal condition. It is the baseline: it shows what happens without the treatment.

The groups that do get the treatment are the experimental groups.

Without a control group, you cannot tell whether the treatment did anything. Plants grow, colds go away, and scores go up over time even with no treatment. The control group shows how much change would have happened anyway.

Note: not every experiment has a no-treatment group. If you compare three brands of paper towel, the brands are compared with each other.

example.prompt: Forty tomato plants are randomly split into two groups. Group A gets a new plant food. Group B gets plain water. After 6 weeks, the tomatoes on each plant are counted. Which group is the control?
steps: The treatment being tested is the new plant food.
Group B does not get it; it gets plain water.
So Group B is the control group, and Group A is the experimental group.
example.answer: Group B, the plants given plain water.

check.prompt: A dental researcher tests whether a new mouthwash reduces bacteria in the mouth. Group 1 rinses with the new mouthwash, Group 2 rinses with a popular store brand, and Group 3 rinses with plain water. Which group is the control group?
options: Group 3, which rinses with plain water
Group 1, which rinses with the new mouthwash
Group 2, which rinses with the store brand
Whichever group has the most bacteria at the end
why: The new mouthwash is the treatment being tested, so Group 1 is an experimental group.
The store brand is still a mouthwash treatment. It is a useful comparison, but the no-mouthwash baseline is the water group.
The control group is chosen before the experiment. Results never decide which group is the control.
check.hint: Which group gets no mouthwash at all?
check.explain: Group 3 rinses with plain water, so it shows how many bacteria remain with no mouthwash. That makes it the control group. Group 2 is a comparison group, but it still receives a mouthwash treatment.

screens.title: Control group vs. controlled variables
screens.html:
These two terms sound alike, and the GED counts on you mixing them up.

Control groupControlled variables
A group of plants, people, or objectsConditions like time, temperature, or amount of water
Does not get the treatmentKept the same for every group, including the control
Example: plants with no fertilizerExample: every plant gets 100 mL of water

Quick test: if you can count it as a group of things, it is a group. If it is a setting you hold steady, it is a controlled variable.

check.prompt: A coach tests whether a sports drink improves sprint times. One group of runners drinks the sports drink; another group drinks flavored water that looks and tastes the same. Every runner rests 15 minutes, then sprints 100 meters on the same track. Sort each item.
check.why: The most common mistake is putting the 15-minute rest or the track in the control group bin. Those are conditions kept the same for both groups, so they are controlled variables; the control group is the runners who get the flavored water.
check.hint: Groups are made of people. Controlled variables are conditions kept the same.
check.explain: The flavored-water runners do not get the sports drink, so they are the control group. The sports-drink runners get the treatment, so they are the experimental group. The 15-minute rest and the track are the same for everyone, so they are controlled variables.

screens.title: Repeated trials and the mean
screens.html:
One trial can be misleading. A tablet might be a little bigger, or one seed might be weak. Scientists repeat trials (or test many subjects) and find the mean, or average:

Mean = (sum of the trials) ÷ (number of trials)

Repeating makes results more reliable. A quick check: the mean must fall between the smallest and largest trial.

example.prompt: Three trials of a seltzer tablet fizzing away in warm water took 61 s, 66 s, and 62 s. Find the mean.
steps: Divide by the number of trials: 189 ÷ 3 = 63.
Check: 63 is between 61 and 66.

check.prompt: A student measured how long a wet towel took to dry. Her four trials were 34, 38, 31, and 37 minutes. What is the mean drying time, in minutes?

mistakes.why: 140 is the sum of the four trials. You still need to divide by the number of trials: 140 ÷ 4 = 35.
You divided by 3, but there are four trials. Divide the sum, 140, by 4.
34.5 is the middle of 31 and 38 (the smallest and largest trials). The mean uses all four trials: (34 + 38 + 31 + 37) ÷ 4 = 35.

check.hint: Add all four trials, then divide by 4.
check.explain: 34 + 38 + 31 + 37 = 140. There are 4 trials, so 140 ÷ 4 = 35 minutes. Check: 35 is between 31 and 38.

screens.title: Sample size and random assignment
screens.html:
When an experiment uses living things or people, two ideas keep it fair:

  • Sample size is how many subjects are in each group. Larger samples are more reliable: 30 patients per group tells you more than 3.
  • Random assignment means subjects are put into groups by chance, like drawing names from a hat. This makes the groups alike at the start in age, health, fitness, and everything else, so the treatment is the only real difference.

If people choose their own group, or the scientist picks who goes where, the groups may differ in ways that affect the results.

check.prompt: A researcher has 80 volunteers to test a new sleep aid. What is the best way to form the treatment group and the control group?
options: Randomly assign 40 volunteers to each group.
Let each volunteer choose which group to join.
Put the 40 volunteers who sleep worst into the treatment group.
Use 78 volunteers in the treatment group and 2 in the control group.
why: People who choose may differ in important ways; for example, the worst sleepers might all pick the sleep aid. Random assignment prevents this.
Putting the worst sleepers in one group makes the groups different before the test starts. Sleep quality becomes a confounding variable.
A control group of 2 is far too small to be a reliable baseline. Both groups need a large enough sample.
check.hint: Which choice makes the two groups as alike as possible, with enough people in each?
check.explain: Randomly assigning 40 to each group gives two large groups that start out alike. Choosing, hand-picking the worst sleepers, or using a tiny control group all let a second difference sneak in or make the results unreliable.

screens.title: Confounding variables
screens.html:
A confounding variable is a second difference between the groups, besides the independent variable, that could also explain the result. When there is one, you cannot tell which difference caused the effect.

The habit to build: before you accept any conclusion, ask "Besides the independent variable, how else were the groups different?"

example.prompt: A homeowner fertilizes his front lawn, which gets full sun, and leaves his shaded back lawn unfertilized. The front lawn grows thicker. He says the fertilizer works. What is wrong?
steps: IV: fertilizer or none. DV: how thick the grass is.
How else do the lawns differ? Sunlight. That is a confounding variable.
Fix: use plots on the same lawn with the same sunlight, and randomly choose which plots get fertilizer.
example.answer: Sunlight is a confounding variable; the sun, not the fertilizer, may explain the thicker grass.

check.prompt: A student tests whether the brand of battery affects how long a flashlight shines. She puts Brand X batteries in a new LED flashlight and Brand Y batteries in an old flashlight with a regular bulb. The Brand X flashlight shines much longer. What is the main problem with her test?
options: The flashlight type changed along with the battery brand, so either could explain the result.
She measured how long the light shined instead of how bright it was, which matters more to most buyers.
She should have tested three brands instead of two.
Battery brand is the dependent variable, not the independent variable.
why: Shining time is exactly what her question asks about, so it is a good dependent variable. The problem is that two things changed.
Adding a third brand would not fix the problem if each brand still went into a different flashlight. The flashlight type is the confounding variable.
Battery brand is what she changed on purpose, so it is the independent variable. Shining time is the dependent variable.
check.hint: Besides the battery brand, how else were the two tests different?
check.explain: She changed two things at once: battery brand and flashlight type. LED bulbs use much less power than regular bulbs, so the new flashlight alone could make Brand X last longer. The flashlight type is a confounding variable. Both brands should be tested in identical flashlights.

screens.title: Placebos and blind studies
screens.html:
People's expectations can change results. If you believe a pill will help, you may feel better even if the pill does nothing. To prevent this, studies with people use:

  • a placebo: a fake treatment that looks, tastes, or feels like the real one, given to the control group; and
  • a blind design: subjects do not know which group they are in. (In a double-blind study, the researchers measuring the results do not know either.)

Then both groups expect the same thing, and any extra effect in the treatment group can be credited to the treatment itself.

check.prompt: In a test of a new headache pill, the control group receives a sugar pill that looks exactly like the real pill. Why?
options: So both groups expect relief, and only the real medicine differs between them
So the control group gets a smaller dose of the medicine
So the researchers can test two independent variables at once
So the study needs fewer volunteers
why: A sugar pill contains no medicine at all. It is a placebo, not a smaller dose.
The placebo keeps the groups alike so that only one variable, the medicine, differs. It does not add a second independent variable.
A placebo does not change how many volunteers are needed; it controls for expectations.
check.hint: Think about what people expect when they swallow a pill.
check.explain: The sugar pill is a placebo. Because both groups take a pill that looks the same, both groups expect relief. If the real-pill group improves more, the difference can be credited to the medicine, not to expectations.

screens.title: Drawing conclusions from data
screens.html:
A conclusion describes what the data show and says whether they support the hypothesis.

  1. Read the data in order of the independent variable.
  2. Describe the pattern: as the IV increases, does the DV rise, fall, or rise then fall?
  3. Compare to the hypothesis: support or do not support?

Be careful with numbers that go down. A falling time can mean something happened faster, so always ask what the measurement means before you judge.

example.prompt: Compost per pot (cups): 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Mean tomatoes per plant: 10, 14, 17, 19, 15. Hypothesis: more compost, more tomatoes.
steps: In order: 10 → 14 → 17 → 19, then 15.
Pattern: the tomato count rose up to 3 cups, then fell at 4 cups.
The data support the hypothesis from 0 to 3 cups, but not at 4 cups.
example.answer: The number of tomatoes increased with compost up to 3 cups, then decreased at 4 cups, so the hypothesis is supported only up to 3 cups.

check.prompt:
A student sprinkled different amounts of salt on identical ice cubes and timed how long each took to melt completely.

Salt (grams)0246
Mean time to melt (min)40312522

Her hypothesis: If more salt is sprinkled on an ice cube, then the ice will melt faster. Which statement is correct?
options: The data support the hypothesis, because the time to melt decreased as the amount of salt increased.
The data do not support the hypothesis, because the numbers in the time row go down.
The data prove that salt always makes ice melt faster.
The data do not support the hypothesis, because the time did not drop by the same amount at each step.
why: Falling times mean the ice melted faster, which is what she predicted. Ask what a smaller time means before judging.
One experiment cannot prove anything, and "always" goes beyond the four amounts tested. Say the data support the hypothesis.
The hypothesis only predicts faster melting, not equal drops. Every step was faster, so the data support it.
check.hint: Does a smaller time mean faster or slower melting?
check.explain: Times fell from 40 to 31 to 25 to 22 minutes as the amount of salt increased. Less time means faster melting, which matches the prediction, so the data support the hypothesis. The tempting wrong answer reads "numbers going down" as "not supported" without asking what the numbers mean.

screens.title: Stay inside the data
screens.html:
A conclusion can only cover what was tested. Watch for three kinds of overreach:

  • Outside the range: a test from 10 °C to 40 °C says nothing certain about 90 °C.
  • Absolute words: always, never, only, proves. One study can rarely back these up.
  • Untested causes: if only light was tested, the data cannot tell you about water or soil.

You may make a careful prediction just beyond the data from a clear trend ("probably faster still"), but the best-supported conclusion is the one that describes exactly what was measured.

check.prompt: Bean seedlings were grown at 15, 20, 25, and 30 °C. Their mean heights after two weeks were 6, 10, 13, and 14 cm. How many centimeters taller, on average, were the 30 °C seedlings than the 15 °C seedlings?

mistakes.why: 1 cm is the gain from 25 °C to 30 °C only. The question compares 30 °C with 15 °C: 14 − 6 = 8.
4 cm is the difference between 14 and 10 (the 20 °C seedlings). Compare with the 15 °C seedlings: 14 − 6 = 8.
You added the two heights. "How many centimeters taller" asks for the difference: 14 − 6 = 8.

check.hint: Find the 30 °C height and the 15 °C height, then subtract.
check.explain: 30 °C seedlings: 14 cm. 15 °C seedlings: 6 cm. 14 − 6 = 8 cm taller. This claim stays inside the data, because both temperatures were actually tested. A claim about 40 °C would not.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• Testable question: names a change and a measurement.
  • Hypothesis: If…, then…, because…. Data support or do not support it; they never prove it.
  • Independent variable: changed on purpose (x-axis). Dependent variable: measured (y-axis). Controlled variables: kept the same.
  • Control group: no treatment; the baseline. Not the same as controlled variables.
  • Fair test: one variable changed, repeated trials or large samples, random assignment, no confounding variables, placebo for people.
  • Conclusions: describe the pattern and stay inside the data.

Routine for every experiment on the GED: label C (changed), M (measured), and S (same, plus the control group) before reading the answer choices.

items.prompt: What is the independent variable in this experiment?
options: The amount of fertilizer each plant received per week
The mean height of the plants after 21 days
The amount of water each plant received
The number of plants in each group
why: Height is what the student measured at the end, so it is the dependent variable. The independent variable is what she changed on purpose.
Every plant got the same 100 mL of water every other day, so water is a controlled variable, not the one being tested.
Every group had 4 plants. Something that is the same for all groups is controlled, not independent.
items.hint: The independent variable is the one thing the student changed on purpose from group to group.
items.explain:

Plant height is what she measured, so it is the dependent variable, not the independent one. The water amount and the number of plants per group were kept the same for every group, so they are controlled variables.

items.prompt: Which group served as the control group?

The treatment being tested is fertilizer. Group 1 received no fertilizer, so it shows how the plants grow without the treatment. That makes it the baseline, or control group.

items.prompt: Read Maria's lab notebook entry. Click the sentence that states Maria's hypothesis.

items.explain:
The hypothesis is the testable prediction: "If bread is stored at a warmer temperature, then visible mold will appear on it sooner…" It names what will be changed (temperature) and what will be measured (when mold appears).

items.prompt: Which statement is best supported by the data?
options: Mean height rose as fertilizer increased from 0 to 15 mL per week, then fell at 20 mL.
Every increase in fertilizer produced taller plants.
Plants given 20 mL of fertilizer per week were shorter than plants given no fertilizer.
The amount of fertilizer had no effect on plant height.
why: You read only the first four groups. From 15 mL to 20 mL, mean height fell from 21.5 cm to 18.0 cm, so not every increase helped.
You compared the 20 mL group with the 15 mL group instead of with the 0 mL group. At 18.0 cm, the 20 mL plants were still taller than the 12.0 cm control plants.
Heights ranged from 12.0 cm to 21.5 cm across the groups. Groups that differ this much show that fertilizer did have an effect.
items.hint: Read the heights in order from 0 mL to 20 mL. Does the height go up every time?
items.explain:
Mean heights in order: 12.0 → 15.5 → 19.0 → 21.5 cm (rising from 0 to 15 mL), then 18.0 cm at 20 mL (lower than 21.5). So height rose up to 15 mL and then dropped.

"Every increase produced taller plants" is wrong because the step from 15 to 20 mL went down. The 20 mL plants (18.0 cm) were still taller than the 0 mL plants (12.0 cm), so that choice is false. Heights clearly changed across groups, so fertilizer did have an effect.

items.prompt: Why did the student grow four plants in each group instead of just one?
options: Using several plants reduces the chance that one unusual plant will distort the results.
Using several plants makes each plant grow faster.
Using several plants allows the student to test more than one independent variable at the same time.
Using several plants means a control group is not needed.
why: The number of plants in a group does not change how fast any single plant grows. Extra plants are there to make the average more reliable.
Every plant in a group got the same treatment, so adding plants does not add a variable. A fair test still changes only one factor.
More plants per group make each result more reliable, but you still need Group 1 as the no-fertilizer baseline to compare against.
items.hint: Think about what could happen if the only plant in a group had a weak seed.
items.explain:
Individual plants vary. If a group had only one plant and its seed happened to be weak, that group's result would be misleading. Averaging four plants makes the result more reliable.

The number of plants does not change how fast each plant grows, does not add a second independent variable, and does not replace the need for a control group (Group 1 is still needed as the baseline).

items.prompt: What is the mean time, in seconds, for the sugar cube to dissolve in 40 °C water? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 246 is the sum of the three trials. To find the mean, divide the sum by the number of trials: 246 ÷ 3 = 82.
You divided by 4, but there are only three trials at 40 °C. Divide 246 by 3.
84 is the largest single trial, not the mean. Add all three trials (80 + 84 + 82 = 246) and divide by 3.

items.explain:
Trials at 40 °C: 80 s, 84 s, 82 s.

80 + 84 + 82 = 246

246 ÷ 3 = 82 seconds

A common error is to add the trials and forget to divide (246), or to divide by 4 instead of 3 (61.5). A mean must fall between the smallest and largest trial, so neither of those can be right.

items.prompt: By how many seconds did the mean dissolving time decrease from 10 °C to 55 °C? Enter a number.

Mean at 10 °C: 182 s. Mean at 55 °C: 53 s.

items.prompt: The student plans one more set of trials using water at 70 °C. Based on the trend in the data, which range most likely contains the mean dissolving time at 70 °C?

Between 55 and 75 seconds
Between 80 and 100 seconds
Between 180 and 200 seconds
why: Every value here is above the 53 s mean at 55 °C. That would mean the hotter water dissolved sugar more slowly, which reverses the trend in every step of the data.
This range sits around the 40 °C mean (82 s). You may have read the wrong row. At 70 °C, the time should be shorter than at 55 °C.
This matches the 10 °C mean (182 s). You read the trend backward; as temperature rises, the time falls.
items.hint: Every 15 °C increase has made the time shorter. By how much did it drop each time?
items.explain:
Mean times: 182 s (10 °C), 121 s (25 °C), 82 s (40 °C), 53 s (55 °C). Each 15 °C step lowered the time, by 61 s, then 39 s, then 29 s. The drops are getting smaller, so the next drop should be smaller than 29 s, perhaps about 20 s. That predicts roughly 53 − 20 ≈ 33 s, which is in the range 25 to 45 seconds.

Every other range is at or above 53 s, which would mean the trend reversed and warmer water dissolved sugar more slowly. Nothing in the data suggests that.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why the company's conclusion is not supported by this study?
options: The groups differed in fitness as well as in drink, so the drink may not explain the gap.
Group B drank plain water instead of drinking nothing at all before running on the treadmill.
The volunteers ran on a treadmill instead of an outdoor track.
Endurance was measured in minutes instead of in miles.
why: Giving the comparison group water is a reasonable baseline; it does not explain why Group A ran 24 minutes longer. Look for a second difference between the groups.
Both groups used the same treadmill at the same speed, so the treadmill is a controlled variable and cannot explain the gap.
Both groups were measured the same way. Minutes are a fine unit for endurance and cannot explain a difference between the groups.
items.hint: Besides the drink, how else were Group A and Group B different?
items.explain:
Group A was made up of college athletes and Group B of people who rarely exercise. Athletes would likely run longer no matter what they drank. Fitness level is a confounding variable, so the study cannot show that the drink caused the longer running time.

Giving the control group water is a reasonable choice, and running on a treadmill or measuring time in minutes are acceptable methods applied equally to both groups. None of those explains the large difference the way the fitness difference does.

items.prompt: Which two changes would make the sports drink study a fairer test of whether the drink improves endurance? Select two answers.
options: Choose all volunteers from one population and randomly assign them to the two groups.
Give Group B a drink that looks and tastes like the sports drink but lacks its active ingredients, and do not tell volunteers which drink they received.
Let each volunteer choose which drink he or she prefers.
Have Group A run on a treadmill and Group B run on an outdoor track.
Tell Group A that the sports drink is expected to improve their endurance.
why: If volunteers choose, fitter people might pick the sports drink, which brings the fitness difference right back. Random assignment prevents this.
Running in two different places adds a second difference between the groups, a new confounding variable.
Telling one group what to expect could make them try harder. Expectations then become a second difference between the groups.
items.hint: A fair test makes the groups as alike as possible except for the one thing being tested.
items.explain:
Random assignment from one population makes the two groups similar in fitness, age, and other traits, removing the confounding variable. A placebo drink that looks and tastes the same, with volunteers not knowing their group, keeps expectations from affecting how long people run.

Letting volunteers choose their drink lets other differences creep back in (for example, fitter people might choose the sports drink). Running in different places adds a second variable. Telling Group A what to expect could make them try harder, which biases the results.

items.prompt: A student wants to test whether the number of hours of light per day affects the growth of bean plants. Which plan is the best experimental design?
options: Grow four groups of five plants under 6, 9, 12, and 15 hours of light per day, giving every plant the same water, the same soil, and 10 mL of fertilizer per week.

Grow four groups of five plants under 6, 9, 12, and 15 hours of light per day, giving every plant the same water and soil but giving the groups 5, 10, 15, and 20 mL of fertilizer per week, respectively.
Grow one plant under each of 6, 9, 12, and 15 hours of light per day, giving every plant the same water, the same soil, and 10 mL of fertilizer per week.
Grow four groups of five plants under 12 hours of light per day, giving each group a different amount of water.
why: This plan changes light and fertilizer at the same time. Any difference in growth could come from either one, so fertilizer becomes a confounding variable.
This plan keeps everything else the same, but uses only one plant per light setting. One weak seed could distort the result; several plants per group are needed.
Every group gets the same 12 hours of light, so this plan does not test light at all. It tests water instead.
items.hint: The best plan changes only the light, keeps everything else the same, and uses more than one plant per condition.
items.explain:
The best plan changes only the hours of light (the independent variable), keeps water, soil, and fertilizer the same (controlled variables), and uses five plants per group so the results are reliable.

The plan that gives the groups 5, 10, 15, and 20 mL of fertilizer changes light and fertilizer at the same time, so any difference could come from either one. The plan with one plant per condition lets a single unusual plant distort the results. The plan that keeps every group at 12 hours of light and changes the water does not test light at all.

items.prompt: The student's hypothesis was: If bean plants receive more fertilizer, then they will grow taller. Which statement best describes how the data relate to her hypothesis?
options: The data support the hypothesis from 0 to 15 mL per week, but not from 15 to 20 mL per week.
The data support the hypothesis for every amount tested, because all fertilized plants were taller than the control plants.
The data do not support the hypothesis at any amount, because the tallest plants were not in the 20 mL group.
The data prove that 15 mL per week is the best amount of fertilizer for all bean plants.
why: Comparing each group only with the control misses the last step. The hypothesis says more fertilizer means taller plants, but going from 15 to 20 mL made the plants shorter (21.5 cm to 18.0 cm).
You judged the whole hypothesis by the last group only. From 0 to 15 mL, every increase in fertilizer did produce taller plants, so the hypothesis is supported in that range.
One experiment cannot prove anything, and "all bean plants" goes far beyond one variety. Amounts such as 12 or 17 mL were never tested either.
items.hint: Check each step from one amount to the next. Did more fertilizer always mean taller plants?
items.explain:
Step by step: 0→5 mL (12.0→15.5 cm), 5→10 mL (15.5→19.0), 10→15 mL (19.0→21.5) all rose, which supports the hypothesis. But 15→20 mL (21.5→18.0) fell, which does not support it. So the hypothesis holds only from 0 to 15 mL.

The tempting wrong answer says every amount supports it because all fertilized plants beat the control. That compares with the wrong group: the hypothesis is about more fertilizer, so each amount must be compared with the amount before it.

items.prompt: What is the independent variable in this experiment?

items.prompt: Which group served as the control group?

items.explain:
The treatment being tested is salt. Group 1 received distilled water with no salt, so it shows how many seeds sprout without the treatment. That makes it the control group.

Group 2 received only a little salt (0.5%), but a little is still some, so it is an experimental group, like Groups 3, 4, and 5.

items.explain:

The first sentence is an observation, the second is background information, the third is the question, and the last two describe the procedure.

items.prompt: Which question could a scientist answer by changing one factor and measuring the result?

This is a history question, answered by looking at records, not by changing a factor and measuring a result.

items.prompt: Sort each factor from the radish seed experiment into the correct category.

Volume of solution in each dish
items.why: The most common mistake is putting the volume of solution in the independent column because it is part of the treatment. Every dish got the same 10 mL; only the salt concentration changed, so the volume is controlled.
items.hint: Ask: What was changed? What was measured? What was kept the same for every dish?
items.explain:
• Independent variable: salt concentration; it was changed on purpose (0% to 4%).
  • Dependent variable: percent of seeds germinated; it was counted to see the effect.
  • Controlled variables: 10 mL of solution per dish, 22 °C in the same dark cabinet, and seeds from the same packet were kept the same for every dish.

items.prompt: Which statement is best supported by the data?
options: Mean germination fell with every increase in salt concentration.
Salt had little effect until the concentration reached 4%.
Seeds in 0.5% salt germinated better than seeds given only distilled water.
Doubling the salt concentration always cut germination in half.
why: Germination had already dropped from 95% to 40% by 2% salt. You may have noticed only the very low 8% at 4% and missed the large earlier drops.
You may have read the table upside down. Germination at 0.5% salt (90%) was lower than in distilled water (95%), not higher.
Check the numbers: from 1% to 2% salt, germination went from 72% to 40%, which is not half (36%). From 0.5% to 1%, it went from 90% to 72%, nowhere near half. "Always" is not supported.
items.hint: Read the germination values in order from 0% salt to 4% salt. What happens each time?
items.explain:
Mean germination in order: 95% → 90% → 72% → 40% → 8%. Every increase in salt lowered germination, so the statement that germination fell with every increase in salt is supported.

The "little effect until 4%" choice ignores the big drops at 1% and 2%. The "doubling cuts it in half" choice sounds mathematical, but 90 → 72 and 72 → 40 are not halvings.

items.prompt: Why did the student use three dishes of 20 seeds at each salt concentration instead of a single seed?
options: Many seeds give a reliable percent; one dead or damaged seed cannot decide the result.
More seeds in a dish make each seed absorb more salt.
Using many seeds lets the student test both salt concentration and cabinet temperature at once.
Using many seeds means a control group is no longer needed.
why: Every dish got the same 10 mL of solution at the same concentration; the number of seeds does not change the salt concentration each seed is exposed to. The extra seeds are there for reliability.
Temperature was kept at 22 °C for every dish. Adding seeds does not add a second independent variable.
More seeds make each result more reliable, but the 0% salt group is still needed as the baseline to compare against.
items.hint: What could happen if the single seed in a group happened to be dead?
items.explain:
Seeds vary; some in any packet will not sprout no matter what. With only one seed per group, a single dead seed would make that group look like 0% germination. Using 60 seeds per concentration (3 dishes × 20) gives a reliable mean percent.

The number of seeds does not change the salt exposure, does not add a second variable, and does not remove the need for the 0% control group.

items.prompt: The student plans one more set of trials with the ramp height at 50 cm. Based on the trend in the data, which range most likely contains the mean distance at 50 cm?

Between 290 and 320 cm
Between 390 and 410 cm
why: This range is about the same as the 40 cm result (201 cm). That would mean the trend suddenly stopped, but every 10 cm increase so far added about 50 cm of distance.
