items.explain:
Mean distances: 50, 101, 151 (from the trials), and 201 cm. Each extra 10 cm of height added about 50 cm of distance (51, 50, 50). One more step from 40 cm to 50 cm should add about 50 cm: 201 + 50 ≈ 251 cm, which is in the range 235 to 265 cm.

The 390–410 range comes from assuming the distance doubles each time, which only happened in the first step.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains why the company's conclusion is not supported by this study?
options: The groups differed in age as well as treatment, so the supplement may not explain the gap.
The volunteers studied the list of words for only 5 minutes instead of a longer 10 minutes.
The results were reported as the mean number of words remembered.
Memory was tested after 4 weeks instead of after 1 week.
why: Every volunteer had the same 5 minutes, so study time is a controlled variable. It cannot explain why one group remembered more.
Means are the right way to compare groups; they reduce the effect of any one person. Reporting means is not a flaw.
Both groups were tested at the same time, after 4 weeks. Timing that is the same for both groups cannot explain a difference between them.
items.hint: Besides the supplement, how else were Group A and Group B different?
items.explain:
Group A was college students and Group B was retirees over 70. Younger adults often score higher on quick memory tests no matter what they take. Age is a confounding variable, so the study cannot show that the supplement caused the 11-word difference.

The 5-minute study time, the 4-week timing, and the use of means were the same for both groups or are normal methods, so none of them explains the gap.

items.prompt: Which two changes would make the memory study a fairer test of whether the supplement improves memory? Select two answers.
options: Recruit all volunteers from the same age group and randomly assign them to the two groups.
Give Group B a capsule that looks like the supplement but contains no active ingredient, and do not tell volunteers which capsule they are taking.
Let each volunteer decide whether to take the supplement.
Give Group B 10 minutes to study the words to make up for their age.
Tell Group A that the supplement should help them remember more words.
why: If volunteers choose, people who already care most about memory might pick the supplement. Their choice becomes a second difference between groups.
Changing the study time for one group adds a second variable. The groups would then differ in study time as well as treatment.
Telling one group what to expect could make them try harder on the test, so expectations would become a confounding variable.
items.hint: A fair test makes the groups alike in every way except the supplement.
items.explain:
Random assignment from one age group removes the age difference, so the groups start out alike. A placebo capsule, with volunteers not knowing their group, makes expectations the same in both groups.

Letting people choose, changing study time for one group, or telling one group what to expect would each add a new difference between the groups.

items.prompt: A student wants to test whether water temperature affects how fast an antacid tablet dissolves. Which plan is the best experimental design?
options: Drop one tablet of the same brand into 200 mL of water at 10, 20, 30, and 40 °C in identical glasses, without stirring, and run three trials at each temperature.
Drop one tablet of the same brand into 200 mL of water at 10, 20, 30, and 40 °C in identical glasses, stirring only the 30 °C and 40 °C glasses, and run three trials at each temperature.
Drop one tablet of the same brand into 200 mL of water at 10, 20, 30, and 40 °C in identical glasses, without stirring, and run one trial at each temperature.
Drop one tablet of each of four different brands into 200 mL of water at 20 °C in identical glasses, without stirring, and run three trials for each brand.
why: Stirring only the warmer glasses changes two things at once. Faster dissolving in those glasses could come from the stirring, so stirring becomes a confounding variable.
This plan controls everything, but one trial per temperature is not reliable. One slightly larger tablet could distort a result; repeat and average.
This plan keeps the temperature at 20 °C and changes the brand, so it tests brand, not temperature.
items.hint: The best plan changes only the temperature, keeps everything else the same, and repeats each condition.
items.explain:
The best plan changes only the water temperature, controls the tablet brand, water volume, glass, and stirring, and uses three trials per temperature so the results are reliable.

Stirring only some glasses adds a second variable. One trial per temperature is not reliable. Changing the brand at a single temperature does not test temperature at all.

items.prompt: The student's hypothesis was: If the salt concentration increases, then fewer radish seeds will germinate. Which statement best describes how the data relate to her hypothesis?
options: The data support the hypothesis at every concentration tested, because germination fell with each increase.
The data do not support the hypothesis, because some seeds still germinated at 4% salt.
The data support the hypothesis only up to 1% salt, because the largest drop in germination came after that point.
The data prove that any amount of salt in soil will kill radish seeds.
why: The hypothesis predicts fewer seeds will germinate, not that none will. Going from 95% to 8% is exactly the predicted pattern.
The size of each drop does not matter for this hypothesis. Germination kept falling after 1% (72% to 40% to 8%), which still supports it.
One experiment cannot prove anything. Also, 90% of seeds still germinated at 0.5% salt, so "any amount will kill" contradicts the data.
items.hint: Check each step from one concentration to the next. Did more salt always mean fewer seeds germinating?
items.explain:
Each step up in salt lowered germination: 95% → 90% → 72% → 40% → 8%. That matches the prediction at every concentration tested, so the data support the hypothesis.

The tempting wrong answer says some seeds still sprouted at 4%, so the hypothesis fails. But the hypothesis only predicts fewer seeds, not zero.

Forty students whose parents signed them up ate the free breakfast every school day for one semester. Forty students whose parents did not sign them up did not receive the breakfast. Many of the parents who signed up also volunteered to help with homework at the school's evening study hall. All 80 students took the same math test at the start and end of the semester.

items.prompt: A man notices that the bananas he keeps in a paper bag ripen faster than the bananas he leaves in a bowl. Which is the best testable question based on his observation?
options: Does storing bananas in a closed paper bag affect how many days they take to ripen?
Are bananas the healthiest fruit to eat for breakfast?
Why do people like ripe bananas better than green ones?
Should grocery stores sell their bananas in paper bags instead of loose in open bins?
why: "Healthiest" is a judgment, and the question has nothing to do with his observation about ripening. It names nothing to change and measure.
This asks about people's preferences, which is an opinion question. It does not name a change and a measurement.
"Should" asks for a value judgment about what stores ought to do. Experiments measure results; they cannot settle what people should do.
items.explain: His observation compares bananas in a bag with bananas in a bowl. The testable question names the change (bag or no bag) and the measurement (days to ripen). The other choices ask for opinions or values, which no experiment can settle.

items.prompt: Which hypothesis was the student most likely testing?
options: If a can is painted a darker color, then the water inside will warm more in sunlight, because dark colors absorb more light.
Does the color of a can affect how much the water inside warms up in sunlight?
If water is left in sunlight longer, then it will get warmer, because the sun gives off heat.
If cans are filled with a larger volume of water, then the water will warm up less in sunlight, because there is more water to heat.
why: This is written as a question. It is the student's research question, not a hypothesis, because it does not predict what will happen.
Every can sat in the sun for the same 60 minutes. Time in the sun was a controlled variable, so this is not what she was testing.
Every can held the same 300 mL of water. The amount of water was controlled, so this hypothesis is about a variable she did not change.
items.explain: The student changed the color of the cans and measured the temperature rise. The only hypothesis that predicts how color affects temperature, in If…then…because form, is the one about darker paint and light absorption. The question choice is tempting, but a hypothesis must make a prediction.

options: the color of the can
the temperature rise of the water
the volume of water
why: The temperature rise is what she measured, so it is the dependent variable.
Every can held 300 mL, so volume was kept the same. It is a controlled variable.

the time in the sun
why: Color is what she changed on purpose, so it is the independent variable.
Every can sat in the sun for 60 minutes, so time is a controlled variable, not what she measured.

options: the color of the can
the temperature rise of the water
the starting temperature of the water
why: Color changed from can to can on purpose, so it is the independent variable, not a controlled one.
The temperature rise is the result she measured, so it is the dependent variable.

items.explain: She changed the color (independent), measured the temperature rise (dependent), and kept the starting temperature (20 °C), volume (300 mL), can type, and time in the sun (60 minutes) the same (controlled).

items.prompt: What is the purpose of the unpainted can in this experiment?
options: It shows how much the water warms with no paint, a baseline for judging each color.
It is the can whose water warmed the most, so it shows the best possible result of the test.
It keeps the amount of water the same in every can.
It adds a second independent variable to the experiment.
why: The unpainted can did not warm the most; the black can did (about 14 °C vs. 7.5 °C). And a control is chosen for having no treatment, not for its result.
The 300 mL of water in each can is a controlled variable. The unpainted can is a group (a control), not a condition that keeps the water the same.
The unpainted can is one level of the same variable, paint color. It provides a baseline; it does not add a new variable.
items.explain: The unpainted can gets no paint treatment, so it is the control: the baseline that shows how much the water warms without paint. Comparing each painted can with it shows the effect of that color. It is not the best result, and it is a group, not a controlled variable.

items.prompt: What is the mean temperature rise, in °C, for the black can? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 42.6 is the sum of the three days. Divide by the number of days: 42.6 ÷ 3 = 14.2.
You divided by 4, perhaps counting the four cans. There are three days of data for the black can, so divide 42.6 by 3.
14.3 is halfway between the smallest and largest days (13.7 and 14.9). The mean uses all three values: (14.0 + 14.9 + 13.7) ÷ 3 = 14.2.

items.explain:
Black can: 14.0 + 14.9 + 13.7 = 42.6. Then 42.6 ÷ 3 = 14.2 °C.

Dividing by 4 (10.65) is a common slip because there are four cans, but the black can has only three values.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Darker cans warmed the water more: black the most, then red, and white the least.
A black can will warm water more than any other container would, on any sunny or cloudy day.
Paint of any color makes water in a can warm up more than no paint.
The black can warmed the water about three times as much as the white can.
why: "Any other container" and "any sunny or cloudy day" go far beyond the data. Only four cans on three sunny days were tested.
The white can warmed less (6.4 °C) than the unpainted can (7.5 °C), so not every paint color increased warming.
Check the math: 14.2 ÷ 6.4 ≈ 2.2, so the black can warmed the water a little more than twice as much, not three times.
items.explain:
Mean rises: black 14.2, red 11.0, unpainted 7.5, white 6.4 °C. Among the painted cans, darker colors warmed more, which is exactly what the best-supported conclusion says.

The "any paint" choice fails because white paint warmed less than no paint. The "any container, any day" choice overreaches, and the "three times" choice miscalculates.

items.prompt: Which is the strongest reason the gym owner's conclusion is not supported?
options: The shake group also got personal training, which could explain the larger gains.
Bench press strength was measured in pounds instead of in kilograms, the standard scientific unit.
Strength was measured at both the start and the end of the study.
The basic plan group served as a comparison group.
why: The unit does not matter as long as both groups are measured the same way. Switching units would not change which group gained more.
Measuring at the start and end is good design; it lets you calculate each person's increase.
Having a comparison group is a strength of the study. The problem is that this group differs in more than one way.
items.explain: The premium members got the shake and three personal training lessons per week; the basic members got neither. Training is a confounding variable that could easily explain the extra strength gain. (They also chose their own plans, so they were not randomly assigned.)

items.prompt: Which two changes would most improve the protein shake study? Select two answers.
options: Randomly assign members on the same plan to get either the protein shake or a look-alike shake with no added protein.
Use more members in each group, such as 40 instead of 8.
Give the shake only to members who already lift the most weight.
Let members switch between groups whenever they want.
Give the basic plan members extra time to lift weights.
why: Choosing the strongest lifters would make the groups different before the study starts, which adds a new confounding variable.
Switching groups would mix the treatment and control, so no one could tell which members actually got the shake.
Giving one group extra lifting time adds a second difference between the groups instead of removing one.
items.explain: Random assignment of members on the same plan, with a look-alike placebo shake, makes the shake the only difference between groups. A larger sample (40 per group instead of 8) makes the results more reliable. The other choices add new differences between the groups.

items.prompt: A woman notices that her houseplants near a humming air purifier seem to have more brown leaf tips than her other plants. Which is the best testable question based on her observation?
options: Does placing a plant near an air purifier affect how many leaves develop brown tips?
Are houseplants more attractive than cut flowers?
Why do some people enjoy caring for plants?
Should every home have an air purifier?
why: "More attractive" is an opinion, and the question has nothing to do with her observation. It names nothing to change and measure.
This asks about people's feelings, which is not testable by changing one factor and measuring a result.
"Should" asks for a value judgment. An experiment can measure leaf damage, but it cannot decide what every home should have.
items.explain: Her observation compares plants near the purifier with plants elsewhere. The testable question names the change (near the purifier or not) and the measurement (number of leaves with brown tips). The other choices ask for opinions or values.

items.prompt: Which hypothesis was the student most likely testing?
options: If a jar is wrapped in a material that traps air, like wool, then the water will cool less, because trapped air slows heat loss.
Does the material wrapped around a jar affect how fast the water inside cools?
If the water starts hotter, then it will cool faster, because hotter water loses heat more quickly.
If a jar holds a larger volume of water, then the water inside will cool more slowly, because there is more water that has to lose heat.
why: This is written as a question. It is the student's research question; a hypothesis must predict what will happen.
Every jar started at 80 °C, so starting temperature was a controlled variable, not what she was testing.
Every jar held 250 mL, so the amount of water was controlled. This hypothesis is about a variable she did not change.
items.explain: The student changed the wrapping material and measured the temperature drop. Only the wool and trapped-air choice predicts how the wrapping affects cooling, in If…then…because form. The question choice is tempting, but it makes no prediction.

options: the wrapping material
the temperature drop of the water
the starting water temperature
why: The temperature drop is what she measured, so it is the dependent variable.
Every jar started at 80 °C, so starting temperature is a controlled variable.

the temperature drop of the water
the waiting time
why: The wrapping is what she changed on purpose, so it is the independent variable.
Every jar was measured after 30 minutes, so the waiting time is a controlled variable, not what she measured.

the temperature drop of the water
the volume of water
why: The wrapping changed from jar to jar on purpose, so it is the independent variable, not a controlled one.
The temperature drop is the result she measured, so it is the dependent variable.

items.explain: She changed the wrapping material (independent), measured the temperature drop (dependent), and kept the water volume (250 mL), starting temperature (80 °C), jar type, and 30-minute wait the same (controlled).

items.prompt: What is the purpose of the unwrapped jar in this experiment?
options: It shows how much the water cools with no wrapping, a baseline for judging each material.
It is the jar whose water stayed the warmest, so it shows the best possible result of the test.
It keeps the starting temperature the same in every jar.
It adds a second independent variable to the experiment.
why: The unwrapped jar actually cooled the most (28.0 °C drop). And a control is chosen for having no treatment, not for its result.
The 80 °C starting temperature is a controlled variable. The unwrapped jar is a group (a control), not a condition that keeps temperatures equal.
The unwrapped jar is one level of the same variable, wrapping. It gives a baseline; it does not add a new variable.
items.explain: The unwrapped jar gets no wrapping, so it is the control: the baseline that shows how much the water cools on its own. Comparing each wrapped jar with it shows the effect of that material.

items.prompt: What is the mean temperature drop, in °C, for the wool-wrapped jar? Enter a number.

mistakes.why: 37.2 is the sum of the three trials. Divide by the number of trials: 37.2 ÷ 3 = 12.4.
You divided by 4, perhaps counting the four jars. The wool jar has three trials, so divide 37.2 by 3.
12.55 is halfway between the smallest and largest trials (12.1 and 13.0). The mean uses all three trials: (12.1 + 13.0 + 12.1) ÷ 3 = 12.4.

items.explain:
Wool jar: 12.1 + 13.0 + 12.1 = 37.2. Then 37.2 ÷ 3 = 12.4 °C.

Dividing by 4 (9.3) is a common slip because there are four jars, but the wool jar has only three trials.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Every wrapping slowed cooling compared with no wrapping, and wool slowed it the most.
Wool is the best material for keeping any hot food or drink warm.
Aluminum foil kept the water warmer than newspaper did.
The wool jar's water dropped only about one-third as many degrees as the unwrapped jar's water.
why: "Any hot food or drink" goes far beyond the data. Only water in glass jars for 30 minutes was tested.
The foil jar dropped 23.0 °C and the newspaper jar dropped 19.5 °C. A bigger drop means more cooling, so newspaper kept the water warmer, not foil.
Check the math: 12.4 ÷ 28.0 ≈ 0.44, so the wool jar dropped a little less than half as many degrees as the unwrapped jar, not one-third.
items.explain:
Mean drops: unwrapped 28.0, foil 23.0, newspaper 19.5, wool 12.4 °C. Every wrapped jar dropped less than the unwrapped jar, and wool dropped least, so the conclusion that every wrapping slowed cooling and wool slowed it most is supported.

The foil choice is tempting if you read a bigger number as "warmer," but a bigger drop means the water cooled more.

items.prompt: Which is the strongest reason the district's conclusion is not supported?
options: Many breakfast families also helped at evening study hall, which could explain the gains.
Both groups took the same math test.
Scores were measured both at the start of the semester and again at the end of the semester.
The no-breakfast group served as a comparison group.
why: Using the same test for both groups is good design; it makes the scores comparable.
Measuring at the start and end lets the district calculate each student's improvement. That is a strength, not a flaw.
Having a comparison group is a strength. The problem is that this group differs in more than one way.
items.explain: Families chose whether to join, and many families who joined also helped at evening study hall. Homework help (and family involvement in general) is a confounding variable that could explain the bigger score gains. Students were not randomly assigned.

items.prompt: Which two changes would most improve the breakfast study? Select two answers.
options: Randomly assign students whose families agree to take part to receive the breakfast or not.
Make sure both groups have the same access to homework help during the study.
Give the breakfast only to students who already have the highest math scores.
Let families move their children between groups halfway through the semester.
Give the no-breakfast group an easier math test at the end.
why: Choosing the top students for one group makes the groups different before the study starts, which adds a confounding variable.
Moving students between groups mixes the treatment and the control, so no one could tell what caused any change.
Giving one group an easier test adds a second difference between the groups and makes their scores impossible to compare.
items.explain: Random assignment makes the groups alike at the start, and giving both groups the same homework help removes the confounding variable. Then breakfast is the only difference. The other choices add new differences between the groups.

vocab.def: Something you notice using your senses or a measuring tool.
vocab.example: Bread on top of the refrigerator gets moldy faster than bread in the cupboard.

vocab.def: A question that can be answered by changing something and measuring the result.
vocab.example: Does water temperature affect how fast sugar dissolves?

vocab.def: A testable prediction that answers a scientific question, often written as If…, then…, because….
vocab.example: If water is warmer, then sugar will dissolve faster, because the particles move faster.

vocab.def: Any factor that can change in an experiment.
The one factor the scientist changes on purpose. Graphed on the x-axis.
vocab.example: The amount of fertilizer given to each group of plants

vocab.def: The factor the scientist measures to see the effect. Graphed on the y-axis.
vocab.example: The height of the plants after 21 days

vocab.def: A condition kept the same for every group so it cannot affect the results. Also called a constant.
vocab.example: Every plant gets the same amount of water.

vocab.def: The group that does not get the treatment being tested; the baseline for comparison.
A group that receives the treatment being tested.
vocab.example: Plants that receive 10 mL of fertilizer per week

vocab.def: One run of an experiment. Repeating trials makes results more reliable.
vocab.example: Timing the sugar cube three times at each temperature

vocab.def: The number of subjects or items tested in each group. Larger samples give more reliable results.
vocab.example: 30 patients in each group instead of 3

vocab.def: Putting subjects into groups by chance so the groups start out alike.
vocab.example: Drawing names from a hat to decide which patients get the new medicine

vocab.def: A second difference between groups, other than the independent variable, that could explain the results.
vocab.example: Fertilized lawn gets sun; unfertilized lawn is shaded.

vocab.def: A fake treatment that looks like the real one, used so expectations do not affect the results.
vocab.example: A sugar pill that looks like the real medicine

vocab.def: A statement of what the data show and whether they support the hypothesis.
vocab.example: Sugar dissolved faster in warmer water, which supports the hypothesis.

notes:
Study Notes: Science Practices

The Steps

  1. Observation: notice something.
  2. Question: must be testable.
  3. Hypothesis: If…, then…, because…
  4. Experiment: change one variable; control the rest.
  5. Data: measure, repeat trials, find the mean.
  6. Conclusion: data support / do not support the hypothesis.

DRY MIX

Dependent = Responding = Y-axis
Manipulated = Independent = X-axis

Check: "The effect of [IV] on [DV]."

Fair Test Checklist

  • Only one independent variable changes.
  • Controlled variables are the same for all groups.
  • There is a control group (baseline) when possible.
  • Several trials or many subjects per group.
  • Subjects are randomly assigned.
  • No confounding variable (no second difference between groups).
  • Human studies: placebo; subjects do not know their group.
TermMeaningSugar-cube example
Independent variableWhat is changed on purposeWater temperature
Dependent variableWhat is measuredTime to dissolve
Controlled variablesKept the sameWater volume, cube size, no stirring
Control groupNo treatment; baselineRoom-temperature water (if testing heated vs. not heated)
Confounding variableA second difference that could explain resultsStirring only the warm cup

Mean of trials: add the trials, divide by the number of trials. Example: (80 + 84 + 82) ÷ 3 = 82.

Conclusions: read the data in order of the independent variable, describe the pattern, and say whether it supports the hypothesis. Stay inside the tested range; watch for always, only, and proves.

Watch out: control group ≠ controlled variables. Never say "proves." Do not conclude beyond the range of data tested.
